# Part 0: Setup

Run the chunk below to load the packages and the three datasets we'll use today. (Every chunk after this one needs them, so start here! It may take a few seconds to load.)

- `bakeoff`: *The Great British Bake Off*, season 14 only (one row per baker per episode)
- `unscaled_cancer`: measurements of breast tumor cells (`Class` is `B` for benign or `M` for malignant)
- `us_castaway_results`: every player from the first 47 seasons of *Survivor* (`finalist` is `TRUE` if they made the final)
- `penguins`: the palmerpenguins data (loaded with the package)

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(ggplot2)

bakeoff <- read.csv("https://stat220-f26.github.io/data/bakeoff-episodes.csv") |>
  filter(series == 14)
unscaled_cancer <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UBC-DSCI/introduction-to-datascience/refs/heads/main/data/wdbc_unscaled.csv")
us_castaway_results <- read.csv("https://stat220-f26.github.io/data/survivor-castaway-results.csv")

head(bakeoff, 3)
```

```{webr}
results <- character(10)

for (k in 1:10) {
  eliminated <- bakeoff |>
    filter(episode == k, str_detect(result, "Eliminated"))

  if (nrow(eliminated) == 1) {
    results[k] <- eliminated$showstopper
  } else if (nrow(eliminated) > 1) {
    results[k] <- str_flatten(eliminated$showstopper, collapse = ", ")
  } else {
    results[k] <- "none"
  }
}

results
```



## Recap: `across()`

Last time we saw that `across()` lets us do loop-type tasks inside {dplyr} pipelines. Suppose we want the *range* of every numeric column and the *number of levels* of every factor column in `penguins`. Here are both approaches. Run the chunk and check that they give the same answers.

```{webr}
# for loop
output <- numeric(8)

for (k in seq_along(penguins)) {
  if (is.numeric(penguins[[k]])) {
    output[k] <- max(penguins[[k]], na.rm = TRUE) - min(penguins[[k]], na.rm = TRUE)
  }
  if (is.factor(penguins[[k]])) {
    output[k] <- length(levels(penguins[[k]]))
  }
}
output

# across
penguins |>
  summarize(
    across(where(is.numeric), \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    across(where(is.factor), \(x) length(levels(x)))
  )
```

# Part 2: `map()`

The purrr package (loaded with `library(tidyverse)`) gives us `map()`, which can replace many `for` loops.

- `.x`: what to iterate over
- `.f`: the function to apply to each element

```r
map(.x, .f, ...)
```

## How does mapping work?

Suppose we have quiz 1 and quiz 2 scores for 4 students stored in a list, and we want the mean score on each quiz.

```{webr}
quiz_scores <- list(
  quiz1 = c(80, 90, 70, 50),
  quiz2 = c(85, 83, 45, 60)
)

map(quiz_scores, mean)
```

`map()` always returns a **list**. If we want the results as a numeric (double) vector instead, we use `map_dbl()`:

```{webr}
map_dbl(quiz_scores, mean)
```

What if we ask for a character vector? Run this one and read the error message.

```{webr}
map_chr(quiz_scores, mean)
```

**Q2.** Why does `map_chr(quiz_scores, mean)` fail?


## The `map_*` family

| Function | Returns |
|:--|:--|
| `map()` | a list |
| `map_lgl()` | a logical vector |
| `map_int()` | an integer vector |
| `map_dbl()` | a double (numeric) vector |
| `map_chr()` | a character vector |
| `map_df()` / `map_dfr()` | a data frame (by row binding) |

# Part 3: A `map` example with the bakeoff data

Back to the warm up. Here's the same task done three ways. The function `eliminated_showstopper()` does the work for a single episode.

```{webr}
eliminated_showstopper <- function(ep_number) {
  bakeoff |>
    filter(episode == ep_number, str_detect(result, "Eliminated")) |>
    summarize(
      n = n(),
      showstopper = if_else(n > 0, str_flatten(showstopper, collapse = ","), "none")
    ) |>
    pull(showstopper)
}

# for loop + function
results_loop <- character(10)
for (k in 1:10) {
  results_loop[k] <- eliminated_showstopper(k)
}

# map + function
results_map <- map_chr(1:10, eliminated_showstopper)

results_map
```

```{=html}
<div class="mcq">
  <div class="mcq-title">Check-in 4</div>
  <p>Compared to the <code>for</code> loop, what did we <em>not</em> have to do with <code>map_chr()</code>?</p>
  <button class="mcq-opt" data-correct="true" data-feedback="With <code>map</code> there's no pre-allocated storage (<code>character(10)</code>) and no index variable (<code>k</code>). Fewer moving parts means fewer places to make mistakes.">A. Pre-allocate storage and define an index</button>
  <button class="mcq-opt" data-correct="false" data-feedback="We still needed the function. A common cost of <code>map</code> is that you often have to write a function first.">B. Write a function</button>
  <button class="mcq-opt" data-correct="false" data-feedback="We still chose the output type: <code>map_chr()</code> is the character version.">C. Decide what type of output we want</button>
  <div class="mcq-feedback"></div>
</div>
```

## `map` vs. `for` loops

| `map` pros | `map` cons |
|:--|:--|
| Don't have to pre-allocate storage | Hard to get used to if you learned `for` loops first |
| Don't have to define an index | Often need to define a function |
| Less error-prone | Less fine-grained control |
| Takes advantage of functional programming | |

For this class, you'll learn the basics of both and practice them on homework. For projects, you can use whichever approach makes more sense to you.

# Part 5: Simulation

Iteration is especially useful for **simulation**. In statistics we often work with a random sample to learn about a population, and we care about the *uncertainty* in our results: did we find a real trend, or could it be due to sampling variability?

## Example: Survivor finalists

If we randomly choose 20 previous Survivor players to play on a new season, how likely are we to get zero finalists? First, here's one random sample of 20 players. Run it a few times:

```{webr}
us_castaway_results |>
  slice_sample(n = 20) |>
  filter(finalist) |>
  count()
```

You get a different answer each time, because the sampling is random. To make results **reproducible**, we can set a seed. Run this chunk several times:

```{webr}
set.seed(0217)
us_castaway_results |>
  slice_sample(n = 20) |>
  filter(finalist) |>
  count()
```

```{=html}
<div class="mcq">
  <div class="mcq-title">Check-in 5</div>
  <p>What does <code>set.seed(0217)</code> do?</p>
  <button class="mcq-opt" data-correct="false" data-feedback="The sample is still random. The seed just fixes <em>where the random number generator starts</em>.">A. It makes the sample less random</button>
  <button class="mcq-opt" data-correct="true" data-feedback="Anything &quot;random&quot; in R relies on a pseudo-random number generator. Setting the seed starts it at the same value, so you (and anyone else) get the same results every time.">B. It makes the random number generator start at the same value, so the results are reproducible</button>
  <button class="mcq-opt" data-correct="false" data-feedback="It has nothing to do with the size of the sample. That's <code>n = 20</code> in <code>slice_sample()</code>.">C. It sets the number of players in the sample</button>
  <div class="mcq-feedback"></div>
</div>
```

## The plan

A single sample doesn't tell us much. We'll:

1. Write a **function** that runs our "experiment"
2. Set up an **iteration** procedure to run our experiment a bunch of times
3. **Analyze** the results

### Step 1: a function that runs the experiment

```{webr}
sample_finalists <- function(n) {
  us_castaway_results |>
    slice_sample(n = n) |>
    filter(finalist) |>
    count() |>
    pull(n)
}

sample_finalists(20)
```

### Step 2: iterate with a `for` loop

Now we run the experiment 1,000 times. (This takes a few seconds in your browser.)

```{webr}
set.seed(0217)

n_finalists <- integer(1000)

for (k in 1:1000) {
  n_finalists[k] <- sample_finalists(20)
}

table(n_finalists) / 1000
```

```{=html}

  <button class="mcq-opt" data-correct="true" data-feedback="20 &times; (126/870) &asymp; 2.9. The most common values in your table should be around 2 and 3.">B. About 3</button>
  <button class="mcq-opt" data-correct="false" data-feedback="That's the probability of <em>no</em> finalists, not the expected number. In this simulation it's small (around 4%).">C. About 0</button>
```

### Step 2 again: iterate with `map`

The same simulation with `map_dbl()`. We need something to map over: here, 1,000 copies of the number 20.

```{webr}
rep(20, 5)
```

```{webr}
set.seed(0217)

rep(20, 1000) |>
  map_dbl(sample_finalists) |>
  table()
```

Each element of `rep(20, 1000)` is passed to `sample_finalists()` as `n`, so the function runs 1,000 times with `n = 20`.

# Part 6: A permutation test

Recall the `unscaled_cancer` data. One question we might ask: is the radius of malignant tumors noticeably different from the radius of benign tumors?

```{webr}
unscaled_cancer |>
  group_by(Class) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(Radius))
```

This tells us the average difference *in this sample*, but we don't know whether that difference is "surprising."

## The idea

A **permutation test** asks: if there were *no* difference between the groups, how big of a difference would we see just by chance?

1. Assume there is no difference between the groups
2. Shuffle the group labels (benign/malignant) at random
3. Compute the difference in the group means
4. Repeat a bunch of times
5. Compare the observed difference to the distribution of simulated differences

If the observed difference is much bigger than the simulated differences, we have evidence of a statistically significant result.

```{webr}
# The observed difference (malignant minus benign)
observed <- mean(unscaled_cancer$Radius[unscaled_cancer$Class == "M"]) - mean(unscaled_cancer$Radius[unscaled_cancer$Class == "B"])
observed
```

## Your turn: run the experiment

**Exercise F.** Finish the function below. It should (1) create a new column `class_shuffled` that is a random permutation of `Class` (*hint:* see the `sample()` function), (2) group by `class_shuffled` and compute the group means, and (3) return the difference in the means. Right now `class_shuffled` is just a copy of `Class`, so the function returns the observed difference. Edit that line so the labels are shuffled.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_perm
permute_diff <- function() {
  unscaled_cancer |>
    mutate(class_shuffled = Class) |>   # edit this line
    group_by(class_shuffled) |>
    summarize(mean = mean(Radius)) |>
    pull(mean) |>
    diff()
}

permute_diff()
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_perm
#| hint: true
# sample(x) returns a random shuffle of the vector x. Which column do you want to shuffle?
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_perm
#| solution: true
permute_diff <- function() {
  unscaled_cancer |>
    mutate(class_shuffled = sample(Class)) |>
    group_by(class_shuffled) |>
    summarize(mean = mean(Radius)) |>
    pull(mean) |>
    diff()
}

permute_diff()
```

Now we repeat the experiment 1,000 times, save the differences, and make a histogram. The red line is the difference we actually observed. (This takes a few seconds.)

Functions you define inside an exercise box aren't saved for the chunks that follow, so the chunk below starts with a complete version of `permute_diff()`. Compare it with yours!

```{webr}
permute_diff <- function() {
  unscaled_cancer |>
    mutate(class_shuffled = sample(Class)) |>
    group_by(class_shuffled) |>
    summarize(mean = mean(Radius)) |>
    pull(mean) |>
    diff()
}

set.seed(0217)
diffs <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) permute_diff())

tibble(
  diffs = diffs
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = diffs)) + 
  geom_histogram(col = "white", bins = 25) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed, col = "darkred", linetype = "dashed")

# proportion of simulated differences at least as extreme as the observed one
mean(abs(diffs) >= abs(observed))
```

```{=html}
<div class="mcq">
  <div class="mcq-title">Check-in 7</div>
  <p>The observed difference in mean radius is about 5.3, and the simulated differences are all close to 0. What does this tell us?</p>
  <button class="mcq-opt" data-correct="false" data-feedback="It's the other way around: a difference as big as ours essentially <em>never</em> shows up when the labels are shuffled.">A. A difference this big happens often by chance</button>
  <button class="mcq-opt" data-correct="true" data-feedback="If there were really no difference between benign and malignant tumors, shuffling the labels would almost never produce a difference as big as 5.3. That's strong evidence that malignant tumors have a larger mean radius.">B. A difference this big would be extremely unlikely if there were no difference, so we have strong evidence of a real difference</button>
  <button class="mcq-opt" data-correct="false" data-feedback="The permutation test can only tell us whether the difference is bigger than what chance alone produces. It says nothing about whether the model is a good one for other purposes.">C. The test doesn't tell us anything</button>
  <div class="mcq-feedback"></div>
</div>
```

**Q6.** In your own words, what is the proportion at the bottom of the output telling you? (Look back at step 5 of "The idea.")

## Function quick reference

| Function | Purpose |
|----|-----------|
| `map(.x, .f)` | Apply `.f` to each element of `.x`; returns a list |
| `map_dbl()`, `map_chr()`, `map_lgl()`, `map_int()` | Same, but returns a vector of that type |
| `map_dfr()` | Same, but row-binds the results into a data frame |
| `rep(20, 1000)` | A vector with 1,000 copies of 20 (something to `map` over) |
| `slice_sample(n = 20)` | Randomly sample 20 rows |
| `slice_sample(n = 1, by = group)` | Randomly sample 1 row per group |
| `set.seed(0217)` | Make random results reproducible |
| `sample(x)` | Randomly shuffle (permute) the vector `x` |
| `table(x) / length(x)` | Proportion of each value of `x` |
